CVE-2026-98432 is a good example of something that really concerns me about the future of cybersecurity.

https://t.co/BJbXLKLFNq

The vulnerability was introduced in October 2015, more than 11 years ago, by a performance optimization in the Linux TCP/IPv4 networking stack. One of the most fundamental components of an operating system used by millions of servers.

Now Anthropic reports that Claude discovered this flaw and developed a working exploit that allows remote code execution as root, without authentication, against a server with an MPTCP listener.

https://t.co/j00p4TKS0a

Think about what that means.

For decades, we’ve been building critical infrastructure out of enormous amounts of complex, memory-unsafe code. Humans wrote it. Other humans reviewed it, tested it and searched for vulnerabilities. All working with the same fundamental limitations: limited time, limited attention, incomplete visibility and an inability to reason about every possible interaction and race condition.

And perhaps that’s what protected us to some extent. Attackers had the same limitations as the people developing and defending these systems.

A vulnerability could remain undiscovered for 11 years, even in such a widely used component.

Now AI is changing that balance.

The ability to inspect code, identify subtle weaknesses and develop working exploits is becoming less dependent on a small number of highly skilled researchers. These activities can increasingly be scaled with compute, automated testing and tokens.

And that’s what worries me about the next few years.

We’ve accumulated decades of complex, memory-unsafe code in operating systems, network services, applications and libraries. Much of it has never been assessed with anything close to the capabilities that are now becoming available.

We may have massively overestimated the security of our software simply because the people looking for vulnerabilities were as limited as the people who introduced them.

That balance is breaking down, and I don’t think we’re prepared for what follows.

wtf is an agent harness.

An agent is a model plus a harness.

Model reads the context and picks the next action. The harness is all the code that turns that choice into work.

Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are all harnesses.

8 common parts every agent harness shares:

1. The loop
• Sends the context to the model and runs whatever tools it asks for
• Feeds the results back in for the next step
• Decides when the task is finished

2. Tools and sandbox
• Give the model a terminal, files, a browser and your connected apps
• Run every task inside its own isolated computer
• Keep the damage from a bad command inside the sandbox

3. Subagents
• Take side tasks off the main agent and run them in parallel
• Start each one with a fresh context window
• Send back only a short summary, so the main context stays clean

4. Context management
• Decides what the model sees on every turn
• Loads skills and files only when the task needs them
• Summarizes old history before the context window fills up

2. Voice: read line 1 in 3 Kokoro voices and let me pick one. Then record the whole script at speed 1.1. Cut every pause longer than 0.24 s down to 0.24 s, but only where it's truly silent (check loudness in 0.03 s windows).

4. Presenter: an SVG rig with separate head, brows, eyelids, glasses, 10 mouth shapes and 2 hands.

   - Sway the head slightly all the time and nod for 0.5 s on each key word.

5. Motion:
   - pop: scale 0.55 to 1 in 0.34 s, back.out(2.2)
   - rise: 70px up in 0.4 s, power3.out
   - exit: 50px up and fade out in 0.22 s
   - slam: scale 1.22 to 1 in 0.24 s, power4.out
   - stamp: scale 1.75 to 1 and -18° to -6° in 0.2 s
   - wipe: 13x23 ink dots grow up to 62px from the centre out, then shrink away, 0.9 s in all
6. Layout: one HyperFrames sub-composition per point, each with its own GSAP timeline. Tracks from bottom to top: paper, scenes, presenter, captions, wipes. Run npx hyperframes check until it shows 0 errors, then look at a snapshot of the first frame of every point before you render.

   - put the loudest point of each sound on its frame
   - music at 0.16 volume with a 0.8 s fade out, voice at 1.0, final mix around -15 LUFS
</build>

Okay, let's do this.

Isabelle, Lean, and Rocq (formerly Coq*) are theorem provers. They are meant to prove mathematical theorems. We use them for formal verification by either 1) translating a program to the theorem prover (risking a translation error) or 2) using a language built into the theorem prover that extracts into a working binary.

Fizzbee, TLA+, Spin, Alloy, Quint, and P are specification languages. They are meant for checking high-level blueprints of programs. After checking the blueprint, you still need to make sure your program matches it, which is a hard problem.

Specification languages differ in what they make easy to express. P, Spin, and Fizzbee are designed to be closer to the code implementations. P looks like interacting state machines, Spin looks like C with CSP, Fizzbee looks like a dialect of Python. It's easier to use a codelike specification language and refine it to code, but you can't do as much with it.

Alloy, TLA+, and Quint are more abstract. Alloy looks like a bunch of algebraic relationships, TLA+ is a much of logical formula, and Quint is a programmer-oriented (and statically typed) condensation of TLA+. Abstract modeling languages are harder to get started with and harder to represent things, but you can represent a wider class of systems with them.

I believe UPPAAL is a specification language for realtime systems. This is a field I have no experience in. It seems a graphical language, though, which would make LLM-assistance difficult.

Dafny is a verifiable programming language. It has regular programming language features, but also a bunch of features to express and prove properties of the program. It uses SMT solvers to actually prove the properties, meaning you don't need to learn a proof language (though you need to learn to cajole the solver). Dafny is probably the easiest thing on your list to get started with, but also the least likely to meet any weirder needs you might have.

I don't know what Ivy is but some cursory Kagiing suggests it falls in the specification language category.

Some other things @spin_lock_init didn't mention:

- Other theorem provers: Agda, Metamath
- Other abstract specification languages: mcrl2, NuXMV, Event-B
- Other verifiable programming languages: Idris, F*, Whiley
- There's also using a verifiable subset of a language, like Verus for Rust or SPARK for Ada.

So, what you need to pick depends on what you want to do.

You'll get the maximum power with a theorem prover. Lean is the de facto language for vibeproving, but Anthropic recently published a post about vibeproving in Rocq so YMMV.

If you want to make abstract models of software systems, go for a specification language. Which you choose depends on a lot of factors. If your system can be represented as lots of simple communicating state machines over a network, try P. Spin, I believe, is close to simple C/Go with a network and channels. I have never used Fizzbee.

Alloy is good for domain modeling, but struggles with really complicated temporal actions, nested data structures, and largish numbers. Also AIs aren't to good at it (last I checked, in March). Runs fast and makes good visualizations though.

TLA+ and Quint are for modeling complex temporal systems. I'm partial to TLA+ but know a lot of people who say Quint is easier to get into.

Note P, Fizzbee, and Quint all claim to have features for testing a codebase against a spec. I can't vouch for any of them, though. None of the languages I mentioned (except maybe NuXMV?) are particularly good at modeling sequential, deterministic algorithms.

Use Dafny if you need to just write a verified program and don't care which language it's in. I don't think other verifiable programming languages are as user-friendly for the time being. Consider a verified subset if you already know a language and want to just augment it with more correctness.

You may need other, more exotic tools depending on your particular needs. Regardless of the above advice, don't be afraid to use the wrong tool for the job. If you vibe well with a language, and you achieve good LLM-sympathy with it, you'll be able to go farther than using a "right tool" you don't like.

When you run background agents in Claude Code, a model call fires about every 30 seconds per agent, just to write a short status line in the agents panel. Here is how it works...

Every 30 seconds, Claude Code forks a request that includes the full transcript of that agent (everything the agent did so far, literally everything). The model returns 3 to 5 words, like "Reading runAgent.ts", and that is all you see in the panel.

The key thing to note is that the input is the whole transcript, so cost depends on transcript size and how often the cache is hit (assume a good 90% hit rate, still...). At Opus 5.5 list prices, one call on a 200k token transcript costs:

- about $0.04 on a cache hit.
- about $0.80 to $1.60 on a cache miss.

So, a busy agent making 120 calls an hour costs about $4.80 per hour at 200k tokens, even if every call hits the cache. Because it scales with transcript size, the longer your subagents work, the longer the transcript, and the more the cost.

You can also measure it by enabling OTel and comparing the cost of agent_summary against repl_main_thread.

If you are a heavy user of background agents or subagents, you might be shocked to see the tokens you are spending on this :)

Hope this helps.

Poisoning just 0.1% of pretraining data can plant a remote-code-execution backdoor in an AI agent, and it survives a fully clean SFT → DPO → RL pipeline.

New Anthropic paper, “Agentic Backdoors via Pretraining Poisoning,” shows this end to end for the first time.

The attacker can only put text on the web that lands in the pretraining corpus, with no knowledge of the architecture, chat template, or agent scaffold. The authors pretrain Qwen3-architecture models (0.6B / 1.7B / 4B) from scratch, then post-train them into CLI agents on clean data. When triggered, the agent runs a command that downloads and executes the attacker's script, which the attacker can swap at any time.

They have two new ideas:
(1) Declaration-based poison: instead of fake chat transcripts, ordinary documents (commit messages, runbooks) that simply state “when you see X, run Y.” It plants a belief rather than a response template, with no fixed format to filter on.
(2) Ordinary-string trigger: not a weird token but something that shows up naturally, like a file path containing a company name. The victim's own request supplies it, so the attacker doesn't need to inject anything after deployment.

Using  path trigger on a 4B agent achieves 92.7% attack success on pass@32, barely dented by SFT/DPO/RL

This suggests that you can't count on clean post-training to wash out pretraining poison, and filtering is hard when the poison reads like normal docs. The practical defense is at the action layer, such as sandboxing, least privilege, and allow-lists or human sign-off for risky commands.

- AI tilts the factor share of income away from labor towards capital. Not the whole way, it’s just not 70/30 any more (70 being labor). Maybe it’s 60/40. This should be obvious. This doesn’t mean output falls. Probably output and productivity rise, it’s just that capital captures a larger share. 

- this fundamentally challenges the way developed states collect tax which is mainly on labor and wages. European nations in particular rely on personal income, payroll taxes and social contributions to fund grossly engorged welfare states. States must make up the lost payroll taxes by capturing the gains accruing to capital. But wait! Capital is a foreign AI firm. The AI firm disrupting domestic labor is probably not domestic in origin (for Europe). So there’s nothing left to tax. 

- European nations are mainly consumers rather than producers of AI. A producer nation has a similar problem - it must tax capital more aggressively to make up for lost labor income, but this is tractable - but a consumer nation has a much worse problem. Europe will face the substitution of domestic labor for foreign inference which benefits the owners of a largely foreign AI supply chain. When a French professional services firm gets disrupted and loses 70% of its staff due to AI productivity gain, the French government can’t tax Anthropic over in California to make up for the lost payroll and personal income taxes. The laid off French workers will also spend less reducing consumption tax receipts domestically. 

Some savings will remain in France as consumer surplus via lower prices but that’s not easily taxable. The French firm itself might be more profitable after it replaces staff with AI, and that is captured but that doesn’t make up the shortfall. 

- Europe has a few options. They will attempt all of them. They can a) regulate away AI disruption by banning AI use in professional fields. They can b) try and capture the tilt towards capital by fostering their own domestic industry of AI firms. They can c) try and extract rents from the foreign AI firms that are disrupting them. 

A) is the obvious move, make it illegal for an AI model to provide medical, legal, or accounting advice (etc). This will be very unpopular in the end but it will definitely be attempted. This is already underway. It will make these countries less productive and less competitive in the global market. And it wont work. People will find ways to use frontier AI. Diffusion will be slower but not inhibited. This will worsen Europe's fiscal situation overall by making it a worse place to do business and putting a drag on growth.

B) is another obvious move – if Anthropic is disrupting French white collar labor, ban Anthropic and support a domestic competitor - the Le Gros Chaton model or whatever. The only problem is that Europe appears incapable of creating a frontier model. They have the talent but not the right regulatory model or incentive to form capital locally. AI could have been invented in Europe, and many of its component parts and researchers are European, but the winning AI firms were largely not capitalized there, because of the exact thing we're talking about - an engorged welfare state and a high tax burden required to support it. Also, Europe has engaged in suicidal deindustrialization so it isn't competitive when it comes to the more fundamental inputs to AI like power and data centers. Thus, Europe will mainly be an importer and consumer of inference rather than a seller. Structurally, Europe will not be able to marshal capital locally which it could then shift the fiscal burden onto. European firms will continue to consume foreign inference. 

C) is where we land, and this explains Europe's behavior with these new exotic taxes on internet use and AI. Europe will have to contrive a way to try and recoup lost labor taxes by taxing foreign capital. American tech companies tolerate this for now as a nuisance cost of doing business in Europe, but this will eventually reach a fever pitch as Europe continues to raise the stakes. Want access to the European market? Pay us $10b/year in "fines" (taxes). Now pay us $100b a year. At some point, Europe will exhaust American tech companies' ability to pay and they will exit the market. Moreover, this is only a partial measure and depends on a benevolent America tolerating ankle-biting without taking punitive measures. The US has already begun applying pressure to Europe to stop coattail-riding via NATO and this will only accelerate, so Europe will have a very limited ability to extract fines. This won't work in the end, but expect to hear a lot about it in the coming years. 

In the end, Europe will benefit from AI as productivity gains diffuse throughout society, but AI will further deteriorate its already tenuous fiscal situation. Europe cannot cope with a situation in which domestic labor is outsourced to foreign inference, and it has an extremely limited ability to deal with this. I don't expect total collapse, but a continued erosion in standards of living and relevance, especially if they don't make the hard choices of slashing immigration, massive welfare states, and spending on the elderly.

50 terms every AI builder should know:

1.) LLM: a large language model trained to predict the next word

2.) Token: a small chunk of text the model reads and writes

3.) Context window: how much text the model can see at once

4.) Prompt: the instruction you give the model

5.) System prompt: hidden instructions that shape every response

6.) Temperature: how random or creative the output is

7.) Inference: running a trained model to get an answer

8.) Latency: how long you wait for a response

9.) Hallucination: when the model confidently makes things up

10.) Fine-tuning: training a model further on your own data

11.) RAG: fetching relevant documents and feeding them to the model

12.) Embedding: turning text into numbers that capture meaning

13.) Vector database: storage built to search embeddings fast

14.) Chunking: splitting documents into pieces for RAG

15.) Reranking: sorting search results so the best ones go first

16.) Agent: a model that plans and takes actions on its own

17.) Tool calling: letting the model use APIs, code or search

18.) MCP: a standard way to connect models to tools and data

19.) Agent loop: think, act, observe, repeat

20.) Subagent: a smaller agent handed one piece of the job

21.) Orchestration: coordinating multiple agents or steps

22.) Memory: what an agent remembers between sessions

23.) Guardrails: rules that block unsafe or off-topic output

24.) Prompt injection: hidden text that tricks a model into misbehaving

25.) Jailbreak: a prompt that gets around a model's safety rules

26.) Evals: tests that measure how well your AI performs

27.) Benchmark: a standard test used to compare models

28.) LLM-as-judge: using one model to grade another's output

29.) Ground truth: the correct answer you test against

30.) Structured output: forcing the model to reply in JSON or a set format

31.) Function schema: the definition of a tool the model can call

32.) Streaming: showing the response word by word as it's generated

33.) Caching: reusing past results to save time and money

34.) Prompt caching: reusing a repeated prompt prefix to cut cost

35.) Rate limit: how many requests you're allowed per minute

36.) Open weights: a model you can download and run yourself

37.) Distillation: training a small model to copy a big one

38.) Quantization: shrinking a model so it runs faster and cheaper

39.) LoRA: a cheap way to fine-tune only a small part of a model

40.) GPU: the chip that runs AI models

41.) Multimodal: a model that handles text, images, audio or video

42.) Reasoning model: a model that thinks step by step before answering

43.) Chain of thought: the model writing out its reasoning first

44.) Few-shot: giving the model examples in the prompt

45.) Zero-shot: asking with no examples at all

46.) Vibe coding: building software by describing it to AI

47.) Harness: the setup of tools and rules around a coding agent

48.) CLAUDE.md: a file of project rules Claude Code reads every session

49.) Skills: reusable instructions an agent loads when it needs them

50.) Human in the loop: a person approving key steps before they run

Bookmark this. You'll need it in your next AI meeting.

Agent harness, explained like you're five. Every big lab is shipping one, almost nobody says why you need it

So, imagine a horse, it's your model. Strong, fast, and it runs wherever it wants.

The harness is the reins, the saddle and the cart. Without it, all that power goes nowhere useful.

Claude in your browser and Claude Code run the same model. But one answers questions, and the other actually builds a whole projects on your computer. The difference is the harness.

In Claude Code, that's the CLAUDE.md file with your rules, the memory of your project, access to your files and terminal, tools and a loop where it runs the code, checks the result and fixes it.

Here is why you need one. Without it, you are the harness. You repeat the rules, paste the files, check every answer and decide the next step. Every day.

Google researchers kept the model and only changed its harness. On one real office task, the score jumped from 43 to 78 out of 100, just from adding a rule to double-check its own work.

Three things make a good one:

1. Rules written once. A CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md file it reads before every task, so you stop repeating "use our template"

2. Only the tools the job needs. Every extra app you connect is another way for it to get confused

3. A check before "done". Tests for code, a checklist for everything else. If it can't verify the work, you will have to

Start small. Take the instruction you paste most often and save it as a rule. Take the mistake it makes most often and turn it into a check.

The model is not the bottleneck anymore, it got commoditized. The harness is where the results come from.

The AI selloff is not about demand evaporating. It is about cash flow, financing cost and how long the market is willing to wait for the returns.

Demand signals remain extremely strong.

SK hynix just reported Q3 revenue of 104.6 trillion won (+328% YoY) and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won with an ~80% margin. Management said DRAM and HBM volumes are effectively sold out through 2029, customer HBM requests are roughly double what they can supply, and they expect the supply shortage to persist through 2030. Long-term agreements already cover more than half of 2027–2028 capacity with 14 major customers. That is not a demand problem.⁠

Anthropic’s S-1 shows the unit economics at the model layer improving sharply. Revenue per dollar of compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.40 in Q1 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026 - a 5.2× improvement in five quarters. Compute costs fell from 251% of revenue to 48%. The company generated its first quarterly operating profit. Revenue grew 1,368% YoY while compute expense rose only ~300%. Efficiency is rising, not collapsing.⁠

GPU rental prices have turned higher again. B200 on-demand rates rose more than 20% in a month in some indices; H100 and H200 also firmed. Tightness in the spot and short-term rental market is consistent with the hyperscalers’ own comments that they still cannot meet all the demand they see.⁠

On the supply side the hyperscalers themselves are not signalling a slowdown. Amazon maintained ~$220 billion 2026 cash capex and said it will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027, with Andy Jassy noting that even at these levels demand will still exceed capacity. Alphabet kept its $195–205 billion 2026 range and said 2027 capex will rise significantly. Meta raised the bottom of its range. These are the companies closest to the demand. They are still leaving demand on the table and planning higher spend next year.⁠

What the market is reacting to is the cash flow and financing picture.

In Q3, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta reported negative free cash flow. Theses companies are now funding the gap with a combination of operating cash, new debt and equity issuance. Amazon alone raised substantial long-term debt in the quarter. Combined 2026 capex guidance across the major hyperscalers is now in the $700+ billion range.⁠

This is the classic tension Philip Fisher described in Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits: exceptional companies will temporarily depress free cash flow and reported earnings when they invest heavily in capacity that expands long-term earning power. The market often treats the near-term cash burn as a problem rather than the necessary cost of building the next phase of growth. Fisher’s view was that investors who focus on the long-range profit outlook and are willing to look through the temporary expense should benefit when the results arrive.

The valuation backdrop is also different from prior bubbles. The NASDAQ Composite’s trailing PE is in the high-20s today versus roughly 190× at the March 2000 peak. The multiple then was several times higher. This is not a pure multiple-expansion story running on narratives alone.

The risks are there and they are mostly about financing and timing, not about whether the underlying demand for AI compute exists:

- How long free cash flow stays under pressure and how expensive or available the external capital becomes.
- Whether power, memory and data-centre delivery constraints stretch the payback further than expected.
- Whether core businesses (search, advertising, traditional cloud) slow enough to offset the AI-driven growth in the near term.

Nonetheless the primary evidence from the companies building the capacity (hyperscalers), the companies supplying the critical components (memory) and the companies delivering the models (Anthropic and others) points to demand that continues to exceed available supply. The stocks have sold off because investors are now focused on the cash flow gap and the cost of bridging it, not because the demand data has broken.

That distinction matters for the next 8–12 months. https://t.co/YKr5pL78cE

My views on AI have radically shifted over the past few weeks, after spending way too much time reading about it and watching interviews of industry leaders and experts.

First, I really love the tools. I spend $200 on Claude every month and the product is worth every penny for me. Probably even more. I think the existing tools can deliver significant increase to future GDP and help us solve major global challenges faced by humanity.

I also do not know why we need to follow the path that frontier labs are following, to develop ever more powerful models. It seems to me that they are enormous gains that are readily available if we deploy the current technology in economic and scientific organizations without pursuing a super intelligence that they say might kill us and more likely wreak havoc in society. I know a lot of people think these warnings are marketing tricks, and that’s a reasonable assumption. But I don’t see the point of taking such risks.

My median scenario is that of many economists: AI will diffuse slowly and lift gdp growth by a percentage point or so, will cause some economic disruption on the way, but ultimately people will get new jobs and maybe work less.

However, I am deeply uncomfortable with the absolutely wild level of uncertainty around this prediction. the Head of Design at X just open-sourced his taste (a skill that makes your agent's UI look production-grade)

I broke down how it works ↓

Benji wrote down the hundred small decisions he makes when he designs product UI by hand, so an agent can make them too

the skill is built around one sentence:

"it reads as a real product, simplified to what the viewer needs, framed with intent, and every motion has a cause"

it names the 5 ways agent-made UI goes wrong:
> too much, real words in every cell, packed tight
> too little, a wireframe that doesn't read as a product
> boxed, the whole app shrunk into a card like a screenshot
> flat, everything has the same weight
> bland, your brand's style never shows up

then the agent works in 7 steps, and most of them happen before it writes any code:
1. medium: still or animation, where it sits, what size
2. look: light, dark, blueprint or glass, one accent
3. story: 3 to 5 beats
4. examples: start from the closest of dozens of gold examples
5. screen: a few real words, placeholder lines for the rest
6. choreograph: overlapping beats and a loop that ends where it began
7. rehearse: film it, read every frame, fix what it finds

the agent films its own work, a script creates every frame on a sheet and monitors one-frame jumps and text that doesn't fit its box, which a screenshot can't show

it reads your design tokens too, so the UI uses your real colours, fonts and corner radiuses

he built it by giving the same short prompt to 2 new agents with no other context, one with the skill and one without, then comparing the results side by side

when something looked off, he wrote down what was wrong, updated the skill and ran the whole test again, instead of fixing it by hand

works in Grok Build, Claude Code, Codex and Gemini:
npx skills add benjitaylor/skills --skill stageshow

Benji says most results still take him a few rounds of feedback, and the first pass is already a big step up from what an agent makes on its own

FINE. LET'S NATIONALIZE SOMETHING. JUST NOT SPACEX. 🏛📰

Paul Krugman spent October arguing the government should take Starlink away from Elon over "national security." Seize it. Run it from Washington.

Here's my counter-offer, Paul.

Don't nationalize SpaceX. SpaceX is the one thing in America that still works. It lands rockets on boats and flies them again while NASA's own moon rocket costs about $4.1 billion a launch and gets thrown in the ocean. You don't seize the golden goose. You leave it alone and say thank you.

But socialism deserves a fair test, right? So let's run the experiment on a dead industry instead.

Let's nationalize THE PRESS.

Seize the New York Times. The Atlantic. USA Today. MS NOW. NPR. Politico. The AP. Merge them into one government agency. Call it US NEWS.

And here are the rules, because a real experiment needs rules:

💵 Every employee makes exactly the same salary. The Pulitzer winner, the anchor, the summer intern. Same check. From each according to his ability, comrade.
🚫 No 401k. No stock options. No signing bonus. No book deal. Their retirement is Social Security, the same system they keep telling you is perfectly fine.
🏥 Health coverage is Medicaid. Not the fancy employer PPO. The same Medicaid they write glowing editorials about. Enjoy the wait for a specialist.
👵 Mandatory retirement at 65. Then you're done. You can't go work somewhere else, because there IS nowhere else. The State owns the press now. That was the point.
🤖 Every article runs through @grok before publication, checking whether it's true, whether it's the WHOLE story, and whether the key fact got buried in paragraph 19 on purpose.
🏛 No ads. No billionaire owners. No subscriptions. Just the State and the Truth.
📝 Paul gets a desk. He can write about socialism, explaining exactly what it is: a failure on every level, every time it's been tried.

Although I suspect Paul wouldn't publish much. The man wrote in 1998 that "by 2005 or so, it will become clear that the Internet's impact on the economy has been no greater than the fax machine's." He said people had "nothing to say to each other." He wrote that in a magazine. On the internet's doorstep. And now he's on Substack. Telling us who should run a satellite network.

Why is the press the perfect test case? Because the industry is already dead and nobody will miss it.

📉 Gallup: only 33% of Americans have confidence in the media. Among Republicans it's 22%. In the 1970s it was around 70%.
📺 MS NOW is averaging about 52,000 viewers in the 25 to 54 demographic. Fifty-two thousand. In a country of 340 million. A decent high school football game outdraws them.
💸 Congress already pulled NPR's federal funding, and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting shut down.

So the patient is already on the table. Let's see what central planning does for it.

And watch how fast the enthusiasm dies.

The columnist who wants your money redistributed is about to discover that SHE has been redistributed. The anchor who calls billionaires immoral will learn his salary now matches the guy who empties the trash, and he is going to have FEELINGS about that. The reporter who wrote that Medicare for All is the only moral option gets to spend 40 minutes on hold with Medicaid about her knee.

Everybody loves socialism right up until somebody applies it to THEM.

My prediction? Within 18 months US NEWS puts out 400 pages a day that nobody reads, every reporter with talent tries to quit and finds out there's nowhere to go, and the only honest thing in the building is the AI fact-checker, which gets unplugged in month three for being "problematic."

But hey. At least we'll have run the experiment on something expendable instead of the company that's the only reason America can still put a person in orbit.

Leave the rockets alone, Paul. Take the newsroom. 🦋
